questions.question: How do you create a channel in Go?
questions.title: Channel Creation
questions.direct_answer: make(chan T) for unbuffered, make(chan T, n) for buffered with capacity n. Both are ready to use immediately — channels are always initialized by make, never declared nil.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand Channel Creation beyond memorized syntax.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Giving a definition without explaining a practical trade-off.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connect the concept to a small production example and state its complexity or failure mode.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Remember: make(chan T) for unbuffered, make(chan T, n) for buffered with capacity n. Both are ready to use immediately.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
A channel is created with make and a channel type:

```go
ch := make(chan int)        // unbuffered
buf := make(chan string, 10) // buffered, capacity 10
```

The type inside the chan keyword is the value type the channel carries — int, string, a struct, another channel, any type. Unbuffered (no capacity argument) means every send blocks until a receiver takes the value. Buffered means sends fill slots up to the capacity before blocking.

One declaration trap: the zero value of a channel is nil, and a nil channel is not a ready channel —

```go
var ch chan int    // nil — sends and receives block forever
ch <- 1           // if this were in a running program: deadlock
```

so channels are always created with make, the same way maps are. A nil channel differs from a nil map though: writing a nil map panics, while a nil channel blocks — forever, silently, with the runtime eventually detecting the deadlock (`fatal error: all goroutines are asleep - deadlock!`).

The created channel is bidirectional — it can send and receive. Directional types (send-only chan<- int, receive-only <-chan int) appear in function signatures as narrowing, but you never make a directional channel; you convert one.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    S[send ch <- v] --> F{buffer free?}
    F -->|yes| B[write to ring buffer]
    F -->|no / cap 0| W[park goroutine in send queue]
    R[receive <-ch] --> F2{buffer has value?}
    F2 -->|yes| D[deliver + wake sender]
    F2 -->|no| W2[park in recv queue]
    W -->|receiver arrives| C[copy sender stack → receiver stack]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
Channel creation is make because a channel is a pointer to runtime structure — a hchan struct holding a circular buffer (for the capacity), send and receive wait queues, and a lock. The nil channel is a null pointer to that structure, which explains every nil-channel behavior mechanically: a send on nil needs a wait-queue to enqueue onto — there is no structure, so the goroutine parks forever; same for receive.

The capacity argument to make is the size of the circular buffer allocated up front:

```go
make(chan int)      // hchan with buffer size 0 — unbuffered
make(chan int, 5)   // hchan with a 5-slot ring buffer
```

That buffer is what makes the two channel kinds mechanically different. Unbuffered (size 0): a send copies the value directly to a waiting receiver — a rendezvous; the sender is parked until a receiver arrives. Buffered: a send copies into the ring if a slot is free and never parks; the value sits until a receiver takes it.

That's why unbuffered channels give synchronization for free (the send completing MEANS the receive happened — no value is ever 'in flight') while buffered channels give throughput (senders run ahead of receivers up to n). Both are created in one expression, but they have different concurrency semantics — choosing the capacity is choosing the protocol.

questions.question: What is the difference between an unbuffered and a buffered channel?
questions.title: When would you use Channel Creation in a real project
questions.direct_answer: Unbuffered: every send blocks until a receiver takes the value — a rendezvous, synchronization built in. Buffered: sends fill slots (up to capacity) without blocking; senders run ahead of receivers.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Unbuffered: every send blocks until a receiver takes the value — a rendezvous, synchronization built in.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The difference is what a send does when no one is receiving.

Unbuffered (make(chan T)) — the send parks the sending goroutine until another goroutine executes a receive on the same channel. The value transfers directly from sender to receiver; nothing is stored in between. The completion of the send and the completion of the receive are the same moment. That's a synchronization guarantee: when ch <- v returns, you KNOW some receiver has your value.

```go
ch := make(chan int)   // unbuffered
ch <- 42              // blocks until someone executes <-ch
```

Buffered (make(chan T, n)) — the send copies the value into the channel's buffer and returns immediately, as long as the buffer has a free slot. The sender only blocks when the buffer is full. A receiver drains the buffer at its own pace.

```go
ch := make(chan int, 2) // buffered
ch <- 1                 // returns instantly — slot 0
ch <- 2                 // returns instantly — slot 1 (buffer now full)
ch <- 3                 // would block: no free slot
```

Executed: the first two sends complete without any receiver existing. With cap 2 and len 2, the third send would block.

The choice is protocol design. Unbuffered when the exchange itself is the synchronization — hand-offs where the producer shouldn't run ahead (a job must be picked up before the next is made). Buffered when you're decoupling rates — a producer that bursts, a consumer that drains, and n is how much slack you tolerate.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    S[send ch <- v] --> F{buffer free?}
    F -->|yes| B[write to ring buffer]
    F -->|no / cap 0| W[park goroutine in send queue]
    R[receive <-ch] --> F2{buffer has value?}
    F2 -->|yes| D[deliver + wake sender]
    F2 -->|no| W2[park in recv queue]
    W -->|receiver arrives| C[copy sender stack → receiver stack]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
Mechanically, the hchan struct has a ring buffer (allocated by make with the capacity), and every send/receive follows the same path:

send: lock the channel. If the buffer has a free slot, copy the value in, wake a waiting receiver if any, unlock, return — fast path, no parking. If the buffer is full (or the size is 0 — unbuffered means a size-0 ring, so 'is it full' is trivially yes), enqueue the goroutine on the send-wait queue and park — until a receive frees a slot and wakes it.

receive: the mirror. A value in the buffer: take it, wake a waiting sender if any. Empty buffer: park on the receive-wait queue.

The rendezvous detail in the unbuffered case: with size 0, the 'buffer' never holds anything — a receiving goroutine's stack slot is used directly as the destination, and the runtime copies sender→receiver when both are present. This is why the unbuffered send completing is a proof of the receive: the copy only happens when both sides exist at the same scheduling point.

The subtle behavioral difference that bites in production: buffered channels defer backpressure. With unbuffered, a slow consumer slows the producer immediately (the send blocks) — natural flow control. With buffered, the producer only feels the consumer when the buffer fills — latency of feedback = n items. Choosing n is choosing how far ahead the system can run before it notices a problem. That's not a performance knob; it's a failure-detection knob.

questions.question: What happens if you send to a nil channel?
questions.title: a common mistake when using Channel Creation
questions.direct_answer: Blocks forever — a nil channel has no runtime structure, so the send parks permanently. If all goroutines end up blocked, the runtime reports a deadlock.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Blocks forever — a nil channel has no runtime structure, so the send parks permanently.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The zero value of a channel is nil, and using it for either direction blocks forever:

```go
var ch chan int  // nil
ch <- 1          // blocks forever
<-ch             // also blocks forever
```

Not a panic — a silent, permanent block. If other goroutines can still make progress, the program runs on with the blocked goroutine leaked. If ALL goroutines block, the runtime's deadlock detector fires: `fatal error: all goroutines are asleep - deadlock!` — the one way this failure becomes visible.

The classic real-world bug: declaring a channel field or variable, intending to initialize it later, and a code path reaches the send before the make. The fix is structural: initialize at declaration (`ch := make(...)` or in a constructor) rather than 'later'.

One deliberate use exists: a nil channel in a select is a permanently-disabled case — select skips nil channels. That's the standard way to turn a case off (setting a channel variable to nil disables that branch) rather than building a state machine of separate selects. It's advanced but worth knowing: nil isn't always a bug — in select it's a switch.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    S[send ch <- v] --> F{buffer free?}
    F -->|yes| B[write to ring buffer]
    F -->|no / cap 0| W[park goroutine in send queue]
    R[receive <-ch] --> F2{buffer has value?}
    F2 -->|yes| D[deliver + wake sender]
    F2 -->|no| W2[park in recv queue]
    W -->|receiver arrives| C[copy sender stack → receiver stack]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
Why block forever instead of panicking like a nil map write? The operations differ mechanically. A map write must find a bucket and insert — there is no honest answer to 'where?' without a structure, and Go refuses to guess: panic. A channel send must enqueue the goroutine onto a wait queue — and 'wait indefinitely' IS expressible without a structure: park the goroutine and never wake it. The runtime treats nil as a wait-queue that never advances.

The asymmetry with nil maps is deliberate design: map-write failure is immediate and needs an error channel (panic); channel-send 'failure' is defined as waiting — the only question is for how long, and nil answers 'forever'.

The deadlock detector: the runtime periodically checks whether ANY goroutine can run. If every goroutine is parked (on channels, mutexes, or waiting for timers), no progress is possible — the program is deadlocked, and the runtime prints the state of every goroutine and exits. That dump is the diagnosis: the goroutine stacks show which channel operation each is stuck on, and a nil channel shows as a nil in the stack trace's argument. The detector only fires when ALL goroutines are blocked — one running goroutine (a timer, a network poller, a leaky loop) hides the deadlock forever, which is why nil-channel bugs in servers present as 'this request hangs' rather than 'the program died'.

questions.question: What are directional channel types (chan<- and <-chan)?
questions.title: compare Channel Creation with an alternative
questions.direct_answer: chan<- T is send-only, <-chan T is receive-only. Created by conversion from a bidirectional channel — you never make one. They appear in function signatures to narrow what a function can do.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: chan<- T is send-only, <-chan T is receive-only. Created by conversion from a bidirectional channel — you never make one.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Every channel you make is bidirectional, but the type system can narrow it:

```go
ch := make(chan int)          // bidirectional: chan int

var sendOnly chan<- int = ch  // send-only
var recvOnly <-chan int = ch  // receive-only
```

The conversion is free and instant — same runtime value, restricted compile-time view. Send-only can send and close but not receive; receive-only can receive but not send or close.

Their real home is function signatures, where the narrowing documents and enforces the contract:

```go
func produce(out chan<- int) { out <- 1 }  // this function only sends
func consume(in <-chan int)  { <-in }      // this function only receives
```

The compiler now enforces the design: produce literally cannot receive on out, consume cannot send on in. Executed: a value sent through a sendOnly reference comes out the recvOnly view — one channel, two restricted views.

The convention to internalize: functions take <-chan for inputs (they consume) and return <-chan for outputs (callers only consume what's given); chan<- marks a function's job as feeding a channel. A pipeline built this way reads as data flowing one direction through typed contracts — the direction is in the signature, and the compiler catches any attempt to swim upstream.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    S[send ch <- v] --> F{buffer free?}
    F -->|yes| B[write to ring buffer]
    F -->|no / cap 0| W[park goroutine in send queue]
    R[receive <-ch] --> F2{buffer has value?}
    F2 -->|yes| D[deliver + wake sender]
    F2 -->|no| W2[park in recv queue]
    W -->|receiver arrives| C[copy sender stack → receiver stack]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
Why does the conversion exist? Because ownership errors are the top concurrency bug class, and signature narrowing is compile-time enforcement of ownership. Without directional types, a consumer that accidentally sends back up the input channel compiles — the bug is a runtime surprise. With them, the misuse is a compile error at the exact function that misunderstood its role.

The mechanics are pure type system: chan int, chan<- int, and <-chan int are distinct types. Bidirectional converts to either direction implicitly; a directional type cannot convert back (once narrowed, the view stays narrow — the original bidirectional variable still exists if the caller kept it). close is allowed on chan<- (the sender owns lifecycle) and forbidden on <-chan (a receiver closing a channel would send the close signal to every other receiver — receivers never own that power).

Standard-library signature-reading, because it calibrates your own: time.After returns <-chan Time (you only consume). time.NewTimer's .C field is <-chan Time (same reason). context.Done() is <-chan struct{} — always receive-only. The ecosystem says: producers expose receive-only views; consumers receive receive-only; the send side stays private. That idiom makes the ownership explicit in every API, and your own pipelines should read the same way.

questions.question: What is the capacity and length of a channel?
questions.title: debug a problem involving Channel Creation
questions.direct_answer: cap(ch) is the buffer size set at make — fixed for life. len(ch) is the number of values currently sitting in the buffer — a runtime snapshot that changes with every send/receive.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: cap(ch) is the buffer size set at make — fixed for life.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Two functions, two different meanings — and the pair teaches what a channel IS:

```go
ch := make(chan int, 3)  // cap 3, forever
cap(ch)                  // 3 — the buffer size from make
len(ch)                  // 0 — empty right now

ch <- 1
ch <- 2
len(ch)                  // 2 — two values buffered

<-ch
len(ch)                  // 1 — one value remains
```

The capacity is set once at make and never changes — it's the size of the ring buffer the runtime allocated. Unbuffered channels have cap 0.

The length is a diagnostic: how many values are in the buffer at this instant. For an unbuffered channel, len is always 0 — values never sit in an unbuffered channel; they transfer directly.

The critical understanding: len is a snapshot in a concurrent world. Between reading len(ch) and acting on it, another goroutine can send or receive, so len's value is stale the moment you have it. That's why len(ch) is for diagnostics and debugging (metrics, health checks, logging queue depth), never for control flow. Deciding 'should I send?' based on len(ch) == cap(ch) is a race — the correct decision procedure IS the send: just send, and let the channel block or not. The channel's own blocking is the only atomic test-and-act it needs.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    S[send ch <- v] --> F{buffer free?}
    F -->|yes| B[write to ring buffer]
    F -->|no / cap 0| W[park goroutine in send queue]
    R[receive <-ch] --> F2{buffer has value?}
    F2 -->|yes| D[deliver + wake sender]
    F2 -->|no| W2[park in recv queue]
    W -->|receiver arrives| C[copy sender stack → receiver stack]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The reason len is advisory-only lives in the channel's lock: every operation (send, receive, len, cap) takes the channel's internal lock, but separately. Your len call and another goroutine's send are two lock acquisitions — nothing composes them. There is no 'len+send' atomic, and adding one would make the API a mini-transaction manager the channel deliberately avoids being.

What len IS used for, honestly: monitoring and load-shedding signals. A worker pool publishing its queue depth (len of a buffered channel) into a metric lets operators see consumer lag — the number rising means the consumer is falling behind. It's information, not coordination.

The cap/len distinction also explains channel behavior classes cleanly: cap 0 (unbuffered — len always 0, every send is a rendezvous), cap 1 (the classic semaphore or single-slot handoff), cap n (the decoupling queue — len measures the momentary imbalance between production and consumption rates). When a system's design uses len meaningfully, it's almost always the cap-n case being monitored; the cap-0 and cap-1 cases have nothing to measure — their protocol is in the blocking itself.
